quote: Ebenso hat man ja in der Theorie der automorphen Funktionen eine Differentialgl. $2^{te}$ Ordn. mit $p$ linear auftretenden Parametern, wo also das Oscillations- theorem hineinspielen müsste
english: Likewise, in the theory of automorphic functions one has a 2nd-order differential equation with p linearly occurring parameters, where the oscillation theorem would therefore have to come into play.
topic: Hilbert sketches analogies between oscillation and eigenvalue theorems and Abelian/automorphic functions, proposes treating singular multipliers of complex multiplication as eigenvalues, and notes that fixing a function by its singularities is a degenerate boundary value problem.

triage.modern_statement: In modern terms: uniformizing a compact Riemann surface of genus p (or a punctured sphere) by automorphic functions leads to a second-order linear Fuchsian ODE (equivalently, a projective structure, written as y'' + (Q0 + λ1Q1 + … + λNQN) y = 0). The accessory parameters λi appear linearly in this equation. The uniformizing (Fuchsian) values of these parameters are the ones for which the monodromy group is real, i.e. Fuchsian. Hilbert suggests treating them as joint eigenvalues of a multiparameter Sturm–Liouville problem. That would let a Klein-type multiparameter oscillation theorem (existence and uniqueness of a parameter tuple for each prescribed set of zero counts) single out, or characterize, the uniformizing parameters. This is a heuristic research programme linking Klein's multiparameter oscillation theorem with the accessory-parameter problem of uniformization. It is not a single sharply stated conjecture.
triage.answered_by: There is no single resolution, so this is partly my own synthesis. The two strands Hilbert connects were each developed later. (a) Multiparameter oscillation theorems of Klein type were proved and generalized in multiparameter spectral theory, including abstract versions in a 1983 J. Differential Equations paper, periodic boundary conditions in the Canadian Journal of Mathematics, and Mathieu systems. (b) The existence of the uniformizing Fuchsian equation was settled by the uniformization theorem (Poincaré and Koebe, 1907; Hilbert's 22nd problem). I am adding this from general knowledge, not from the searches. Explicit determination of the accessory parameters is still unsolved in general. Their best-known modern characterization is Takhtajan–Zograf (1980s): the accessory parameters are derivatives of the classical Liouville action, not an oscillation-theorem characterization. I found no source showing that Hilbert's specific oscillation-theorem route to the automorphic accessory parameters was carried out.

evidence.claim: Abstract analogues of Klein's oscillation theorem were proved for multiparameter eigenvalue problems, showing that eigenpairs with a given index exist (and in some cases are unique).
Klein's oscillation theorem was extended to multiparameter systems of linear ODEs with periodic boundary conditions.
A Klein oscillation theorem holds for the multiparameter Mathieu system, showing the theory is still in use.
Historically, the oscillation theorem was shown for equations more general than Lamé's, following Klein's late-19th-century work on multiparameter problems.
The accessory parameters of the Fuchsian uniformization are linked to the classical Liouville action (Takhtajan–Zograf), and this is still being extended, e.g. to orbifold Riemann surfaces.
Takhtajan–Teo describe a non-trivial relation between the accessory parameters of the Fuchsian uniformization of the punctured sphere and the classical Liouville action.
Lamé equations and automorphic functions were historically connected through linear ODEs and Fuchsian groups (Poincaré).

triage.why: The note is a short analogy, not a precise statement. It most plausibly refers to the accessory parameters of the uniformizing Fuchsian ODE and to Klein's multiparameter oscillation theorem, which was well known in Göttingen at the time. Both areas were developed later: multiparameter oscillation theory is still researched, and the existence of uniformizing equations was settled in 1907 (from my general knowledge, not the searches). That is why I chose 'solved' for the broad programme. Explicitly computing accessory parameters is still an open, active topic, but it is now approached through the Liouville action rather than oscillation theorems. My searches turned up no paper that carries out Hilbert's oscillation-theorem idea for automorphic functions. I also could not confirm whether Hilbert himself or E. Hilb pursued it in print, because the search limit cut off further checks. So 'possibly_unexplored' or 'open_and_known' could fit the narrow version of the idea, and I keep confidence low.
